title: Reverse Bits
description: Brute force to optimized: string reversal versus direct bitwise shifting versus a byte wise lookup table.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
Problem Summary: Given a 32 bit unsigned integer, reverse the order of its bits and return the resulting integer.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem
Given a 32 bit unsigned integer, reverse the order of its bits and return the resulting integer.

blocks.title: Analogy: Reading a Row of Lights Backward
blocks.text: Like reading a row of 32 on-off lights from right to left instead of left to right, producing a mirror image of the original pattern.

blocks.caption: The bits of the number are mirrored end to end

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Reading the 32 bits from right to left instead of left to right","00111001011110000010100101000000","mirroring the bit string end to end swaps the position of every bit with its mirror partner"],["As a decimal integer","964176192","the mirrored binary string interpreted as an unsigned 32 bit value"]]}

{"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["A single 1 at the very last position moves to the very first position when mirrored","10000000000000000000000000000000","mirroring swaps position 31 (the lowest bit) with position 0 (the highest bit)"],["As a decimal integer","2147483648","a single 1 at the highest bit position of an unsigned 32 bit integer"]]}

blocks.text: Edge case: n = 0
A value of all zero bits mirrors to itself, since there is nothing to rearrange, giving 0.
5. How Should We Think?
It helps to ask whether converting to a string is really necessary just to reverse an ordering, or whether the same mirroring can happen directly on the bits themselves.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The brute force converts n to a string, reverses the string using a general purpose string reversal, and parses it back, paying string conversion overhead on both ends for something that is fundamentally just bit reordering.

Observation 2: A bit reversal can be built directly, one bit at a time, since extracting the lowest bit of n and shifting it into the result from the other end mirrors the position exactly as a full string reversal would, without ever leaving integer arithmetic.

Observation 3: If this same reversal needs to be repeated many times (for example across many calls), doing 32 individual bit operations every single time is itself repeated work; splitting the 32 bits into 4 independent 8 bit bytes and precomputing the reversed form of all 256 possible bytes ONCE turns every future call into just 4 table lookups and a reassembly.

Observation 4: Tracing an 8 bit value n = 00000011 confirms the direct bitwise approach, extracting its two lowest 1 bits and shifting them into the result produces 11000000 after only 2 meaningful steps, with the remaining 6 steps contributing nothing since the rest of n is already 0.

Recognizing that bit reversal can be done with pure shifting instead of string conversion, and that a bounded domain like a single byte is small enough to fully precompute, is what carries this problem from a string trick to a genuine O(1) technique.
6. Brute Force Solution
Convert the number to its 32 character binary string representation, reverse that string directly, then parse the reversed string back into an integer.
Step by step algorithm

items: Convert n to a 32 character binary string, padding with leading zeros as needed.
Reverse that string.
Parse the reversed string back into an integer.

codes.python:
def reverse_bits(n):
    binary_string = format(n, '032b')                          # convert to a 32 character binary string
    reversed_string = binary_string[::-1]
    return int(reversed_string, 2)                                # parse the reversed string back into an integer


if __name__ == "__main__":
    n = 3
    print(reverse_bits(n))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The binary string is explicitly padded to exactly 32 characters, since a naive conversion would drop leading zeros and silently produce a shorter, wrongly aligned string.
A general purpose string reversal is used since, at this stage, the problem is being treated as a string manipulation task rather than a bitwise one.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Reversing the string representation of the bits and parsing it back correctly produces the bit reversed integer.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(32), for building, reversing, and reparsing the string.
Space: O(32), for the string representations.
Limitation: converting to and from a string representation adds overhead that pure bitwise operations can avoid entirely.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the brute force works but is wasteful: it pays for a full string conversion and a full string reversal just to reorder 32 bits, when bitwise operations can reorder them directly.

What direct bit extraction fixes: pulling the lowest bit of n and shifting it into the result 32 times reproduces the exact same mirrored ordering, without ever building a string.

What remains wasteful if this repeats often: even the pure bitwise version still does 32 individual operations every single call, none of which are reused across calls.

The core idea for this stage: replace string conversion with 32 direct shift-and-mask operations, keeping the door open for an even faster approach if the operation repeats often.

Build the reversed integer directly using bitwise operations. Repeat 32 times: extract the lowest bit of n, shift the result left by one to make room, OR in the extracted bit, and shift n right by one to expose its next bit. After 32 iterations, the result holds every bit of n in mirrored order.
9. Optimized Solution
Extract each bit of n from the lowest position and shift it directly into the result, one bit at a time (shown here on an 8 bit example for clarity).
Dry run for an 8 bit value n = 00000011 (decimal 3)

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Extracted bit","Result so far"],"rows":[["1","1 (lowest bit of n)","00000001"],["2","1 (next lowest bit)","00000011"],["3 through 8","0 (every remaining bit)","11000000, unchanged after this since all remaining bits are 0"]]}

blocks.caption: Optimized: extract the lowest bit and shift it into the result, 32 times over

blocks.text: Why This Works

Each of the 32 iterations moves the current lowest bit of n into what becomes, after all shifts complete, the mirrored position on the opposite end of the result, so after exactly 32 iterations every bit has been relocated to its correctly mirrored position.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens","Result"],"rows":[["The extracted bit is 0","Result is shifted left and OR-ed with 0, effectively just making room","That mirrored position correctly stays 0"],["The extracted bit is 1","Result is shifted left and OR-ed with 1","That mirrored position correctly becomes 1"]]}

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(32), a fixed number of pure bitwise operations.
Space: O(1), no string conversion needed.
Code walkthrough

items: The result is built up by shifting it left before OR-ing in each new bit, which is exactly what places earlier extracted bits into higher positions over time.
An unsigned right shift is used on n so that bits shifted in from the left are always 0, never accidentally sign-extended 1s.

blocks.text: 10. Further Optimization: Byte Wise Lookup Table

The 32 bit number can be split into 4 separate 8 bit bytes. If the bit reversed value of every possible byte (0 through 255) is precomputed once into a lookup table, then reversing any 32 bit number only requires looking up the reversed version of each of its 4 bytes and reassembling them in reverse byte order, replacing 32 individual bit operations with just 4 table lookups.
Dry run conceptual outline

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result"],"rows":[["Split n into 4 bytes: byte0 (bits 0 to 7), byte1 (bits 8 to 15), byte2 (bits 16 to 23), byte3 (bits 24 to 31)","four independent 8 bit values"],["Look up each byte's bit reversed version in the precomputed table","reversedByte0, reversedByte1, reversedByte2, reversedByte3"],["Reassemble in reverse byte order: reversedByte0 becomes the highest byte, reversedByte3 becomes the lowest","the final 32 bit reversed result"]]}

blocks.caption: Further optimization: reverse each of the 4 bytes via a precomputed table, then reassemble in reverse order

codes.python:
# precomputed once, outside any single call
byte_reverse_table = [0] * 256
for b in range(256):
    reversed_byte = 0
    value = b
    for _ in range(8):
        reversed_byte = (reversed_byte << 1) | (value & 1)
        value >>= 1
    byte_reverse_table[b] = reversed_byte


def reverse_bits(n):
    byte0 = n & 0xFF
    byte1 = (n >> 8) & 0xFF
    byte2 = (n >> 16) & 0xFF
    byte3 = (n >> 24) & 0xFF
    return (byte_reverse_table[byte0] << 24) | (byte_reverse_table[byte1] << 16) | \
           (byte_reverse_table[byte2] << 8) | byte_reverse_table[byte3]           # reassembled in reverse byte order


if __name__ == "__main__":
    n = 3
    print(reverse_bits(n))

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: The 256 entry table is built exactly once, outside the function that handles individual calls, since rebuilding it per call would defeat its entire purpose.
Each byte is extracted with a mask and shift, looked up independently, then placed into its mirrored byte position (byte0 becomes the highest byte of the result, and so on) during reassembly.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1), just 4 table lookups per call (the table itself is built once, not per call).
Space: O(1) additional per call, plus a fixed 256 entry table shared across all calls.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

This problem is a clean showcase of the classic time-space trade off in bit manipulation: precomputing a small lookup table for a limited domain (all 256 possible byte values) turns a per-call linear scan into a handful of constant time lookups whenever the same operation is repeated many times.
Common Mistakes

items: Using a signed right shift in languages that distinguish it, which can shift in 1s instead of 0s and silently corrupt the result.
Rebuilding the byte reversal lookup table inside the function on every single call, which defeats the entire point of precomputing it once.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["n equal to 0","Reverses to itself."],["n with all 32 bits set","Also reverses to itself, since a fully symmetric pattern is unaffected by mirroring."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips

Mention the byte wise lookup table as the natural follow up once asked to optimize further, since it demonstrates the broader idea of trading a small amount of precomputed memory for a large repeated speedup.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid the string conversion", think: direct bit extraction and shifting instead.
If the interviewer says "what if this function is called many times", think: precompute a byte wise lookup table once, reuse it across all calls.
If the interviewer says "how would you reverse just part of the bits", think: the same shift-and-mask idea applied to a smaller bit range.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: Why does building the lookup table once, outside the function, matter for its time complexity claim?
How would you extend the byte wise lookup table approach to a 64 bit integer?
What would happen if a signed right shift were used instead of an unsigned one in the optimized solution?
Why is a single byte (256 possible values) a practical size to fully precompute, while all 32 bit values would not be?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Number of 1 Bits and Counting Bits, which also manipulate individual bits directly rather than through string conversion.
Any "precompute a lookup table for a bounded domain" technique, the same trade off used in problems that repeatedly query a small, fixed universe of possible inputs.
Two Sum and other hash-map-based problems, which share the general spirit of trading memory for speed, just with a hash map instead of an array-indexed table.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force (string reversal): O(32) time, O(32) space.
Optimized (bitwise shifting): O(32) time, O(1) space.
Further optimized (byte wise lookup table): O(1) time per call, O(1) space per call plus a shared 256 entry table.
13. Final Summary

items: Pattern: bit by bit extraction and reinsertion, further optimized with a precomputed byte wise lookup table.

Core Idea: bit reversal can be done with pure shifting instead of string conversion, and splitting the 32 bits into small, fully precomputable bytes turns repeated calls into constant time table lookups.
Time: O(32) for both the brute force and the bitwise optimized version, O(1) per call for the byte wise lookup table.
Space: O(32) for the brute force, O(1) for the bitwise version, O(1) per call plus a shared 256 entry table for the lookup version.
Most Important Observation: a small, bounded domain like a single byte, with only 256 possible values, is cheap enough to fully precompute once and reuse forever.
Interview Difficulty: the bitwise version is the expected default; proposing the byte wise lookup table unprompted signals awareness of amortized cost across repeated calls.
One line memory trick: shift bits directly to reverse them, or precompute all 256 byte reversals once to make it instant.
